findings.title: Federated recovery-code credential cannot track used codes, enabling code reuse
findings.body: getCredential() now prefers the credential returned from the federated (user storage) credentials stream. Callers treat the result as a stateful RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean uses getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() to decide which code to ask for, and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById() when all codes are used. For a federated credential there is no local row, so removeStoredCredentialById() is a no-op and the provider is never told that a code was consumed (e.g. BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials() always rebuilds the model from the raw list with no 'used' state). Consequence: the login form always requests code #0 and the same recovery code remains valid indefinitely — one-time codes become reusable, which defeats their security purpose.

findings.title: Raw recovery codes are sent to user storage as plaintext JSON
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the full list of generated raw (unhashed) recovery codes into JSON and passes it as the UserCredentialModel value to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). Any user storage provider that supports the recovery-authn-codes type will receive and most likely persist the codes in clear text (as the test provider does). Local storage stores only salted hashes, so this is a significant weakening of the credential handling contract and should at least be documented/hashed before being handed off.

findings.title: No feedback when neither user storage nor local creation succeeds / credential ID lost
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential returns void and swallows the outcome: if updateCredential() returns false, it unconditionally creates the credential locally, but it never reports whether the operation actually succeeded, and the caller (RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction) calls reqActionContext.success() regardless. A failing provider (e.g. it accepted the type but discarded the value) would leave the user without usable recovery codes while the required action is marked complete.

findings.title: getCredentials() dereferences possibly null MyUser
findings.body: getMyUser(user) returns users.get(...) which can be null (other methods in this class explicitly null-check it, e.g. isConfiguredFor and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream). Accessing myUser.recoveryCodes immediately afterwards will throw NullPointerException for any user not present in the in-memory map (e.g. a stale cached federated user), breaking credential listing.

findings.title: Optional.get() without presence check can throw NoSuchElementException
findings.body: credentialModelOpt.get() is invoked unconditionally. If neither the federated nor the local store holds a recovery-codes credential (e.g. the credential was removed between authentication steps), this throws NoSuchElementException during form rendering, producing a 500 error instead of a graceful login failure. Handle the empty Optional explicitly.

findings.title: Test does not verify code consumption or exhaustion behaviour
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only logs in once with code #0. It does not assert that a used code is rejected on a subsequent login, nor that the prompted code number advances, which is exactly the behaviour that is broken for federated credentials. Adding a second login attempt with the same code would catch the reuse problem.
